claims.text: The initial Fe-Co-Ni-Ti high-entropy alloy is a single-phase fcc material.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloys have coercivity below 50 Oe.
Low coercivity in single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloys results from suppressed orbital moments caused by delocalized 3d states.
Aging at 600–800 °C can induce Ti-rich secondary-phase precipitation in an fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti matrix.
The Ti-rich secondary phases may be TiFe or TiNi intermetallics.
The precipitates can be nanoscale and coherent or semi-coherent with the fcc matrix.
Ti-rich precipitation can occur without disrupting the stability or integrity of the fcc matrix.
Ti-rich precipitate interfaces induce local lattice strain around neighboring Fe, Co, and Ni atoms.
Lattice strain at precipitate interfaces modifies the magnetic electronic environment of neighboring Fe, Co, and Ni atoms.
The precipitate-induced strain reduces the bandwidth of 3d electrons.
Reduced 3d bandwidth restores or localizes orbital magnetic moments.
Enhanced orbital-moment localization strengthens magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Exchange coupling at fcc/precipitate interfaces creates domain-wall pinning sites.
Interfacial pinning and altered magnetic coupling increase coercivity.
The precipitate-containing alloy will achieve coercivity exceeding 100 Oe.
The precipitate-containing alloy will retain a magnetic ordering temperature above 500 K.
Ti concentration must remain below the solubility limit for secondary-phase formation to avoid transformation to non-magnetic or brittle phases.
Precipitate identity and size distribution depend on processing conditions and can affect the magnitude of coercivity enhancement.
Rapid quenching can provide a single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti control sample against which an aged dual-phase sample can be compared.
TEM and APT can distinguish fine-scale phase separation from an apparently single-phase microstructure.

contradictions.description: The intervention requires Ti-rich secondary-phase precipitation, while the boundary says Ti must remain below the solubility limit for secondary-phase formation. If 'solubility limit' has its conventional meaning, remaining below it suppresses rather than promotes precipitation.

The predicted ordering temperature is above 500 K, but the stated temperature-based falsifier only rejects the hypothesis if ordering falls significantly below room temperature. An observed ordering temperature between room temperature and 500 K would violate the prediction without satisfying the stated falsification criterion.
